proxy_language: Proto-Mongolic (with Proto-Tungusic as secondary comparison); no attested language is known for Palaeolithic Transbaikal and Mongolia
proxy_rationale: The late Palaeolithic microblade groups (c. 20-12 kya, e.g. Khotyk, Ust-Menza, Mongolian Tolbor and Khanzat industries) left no linguistic record. The region's later languages are Mongolic, Tungusic and Turkic, but these are Holocene-era expansions and the Altaic relationship is contested, so any proxy is a purely game-level convenience. Proto-Mongolic (reconstructed via Middle Mongol, Secret History, Khalkha, Buryat) is used as the most defensible regional stand-in, since it is a well-reconstructed language of the same geography. The link to Pleistocene populations is extremely weak and carries no claim of continuity.
phonology: Proto-/Middle Mongolic consonants: stops *p *b *t *d *k *g (and *q, *G in back-vowel words), affricates *c(ch) *j, fricatives *s *š *h/x, nasals *m *n *ŋ, liquids *l *r, glides *y *w. Vowels: *a *e *i *o *u *ö *ü, with long vowels (aa, ee, ii, oo, uu, öö, üü) and diphthongs (ai, oi, ui, ei, üi). Vowel harmony: back (a o u) vs front (e ö ü), i neutral; Middle Mongol also shows rounding/labial harmony. Initial *p- is lost or becomes h/f in modern languages but is kept in Middle Mongol/Proto-Mongolic reconstruction.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes: V, CV, VC, CVC (CVV, CVVC with long vowels/diphthongs). Word-initial: single consonant or vowel; no initial clusters, and *r- and *l- are avoided word-initially in native words. Word-medial clusters limited to two consonants (e.g. -rt-, -lb-, -nt-, -gd-, -ms-). Word-final consonants: n, r, l, g/k, s, d/t, b, m, ng; no final clusters in native roots. Vowel harmony governs every word, so names should keep one harmonic class (back or front), allowing i freely. Stress is weak and initial and does not affect spelling.
orthography: Latinised scholarly transliteration of Middle Mongol/Mongolian: plain letters a b c d e g h i j k l m n o p q r s t u w y; ö ü for front rounded vowels; š written 'sh' or š, c as 'ch', ŋ as 'ng'. Long vowels doubled (aa, ee, oo, uu, öö, üü). Use g for velar stop (not 'gh'), x or h for the velar/glottal fricative.
morphology: Agglutinative, suffixing only. Nominal roots are bare stems; plural suffixes -d, -s, -nar, -ud/-üd; case suffixes include genitive -n/-iin/-un/-ün, accusative -i, dative-locative -da/-de, ablative -aas/-ees, instrumental -aar/-eer, comitative -tai/-tei. Denominal noun suffixes: -či/-chi (agent, 'one who does/has'), -tu/-tü and -tai/-tei (having, possessing), -gai/-ei (diminutive-ish), -sun/-sün (product nouns), -l, -lig. Verbal nouns: -l (e.g. product of action), -ga/-ge, -ma/-me, -gči agent. Reduplication is rare and restricted to intensifiers and onomatopoeia.
compounding: Modifier precedes head. Genitive constructions place the possessor first: 'X-n Y' = 'Y of X' (genitive -n/-iin/-un/-ün on the possessor, or sometimes a bare juxtaposed compound with no case). Denominal agent nouns use -či (e.g. 'hunter' = hunt-er: aduuči from *adu-). Possessive/privative adjectives use -tai/-gui ('with'/'without'). Names like 'River Stew' are formed as modifier + head compounds (mören + shöl) or genitive phrases.
noun_phrase_order: Strictly head-final: adjective/modifier before noun, possessor before possessed, numeral before noun, demonstrative before noun (e.g. cagaan morin 'white horse'; ger-iin ömnö 'in front of the tent').

notes: Highly speculative: no linguistic continuity from Pleistocene microblade makers to Mongolic speakers is established; Proto-Mongolic is a phonological and morphological flavour proxy only. Words are not identical to Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx words; no word may be identical to a word of those Goidelic languages (the proxy is not Goidelic). Keep one vowel-harmony class per word where possible, avoid initial r- and l-, and avoid f, v, z which are absent from native Mongolic roots. The existing game strings (e.g. Jilhuh, Dilwil) have non-Mongolic shapes such as unharmonised or initial-l patterns and should be rebuilt with harmonic CV(C) syllables and the compound/genitive patterns above.
